what: Kanzhun operates BOSS Zhipin, the largest online recruitment platform in China. Its distinguishing feature is that job seekers chat directly with the hiring manager in the app rather than sending a CV into a company’s recruitment system. Employers pay to post jobs and to reach candidates.
customers: Chinese employers, from small businesses to large corporations, who pay for job postings and candidate access, and job seekers who use the app free of charge.
money: Online recruitment services to enterprise customers
Subscriptions and pay-per-use fees for job posting, candidate search and messaging.
Advertising and other smaller revenue lines.
moat: This is a two-sided marketplace with the strongest possible network effect: employers go where the candidates are and candidates go where the jobs are, and BOSS Zhipin has by far the most of both. The direct-chat model also gets faster responses than CV-based rivals, which is the reason users prefer it. Mobile-first design and enormous brand awareness in China make the position very difficult to attack.
risks: Revenue depends on Chinese hiring activity, which has been weak: revenue was flat from $668.4M in 2021 to $654.0M in 2022 during the downturn.
Chinese internet companies carry regulatory risk that is difficult for an outside investor to assess, and recruitment platforms hold large amounts of personal data.
This is a US-listed holding company structure over Chinese operating entities, which means the shares are not direct ownership of the business in the way they would be for a US company.
Youth unemployment in China is high, which means many candidates and fewer paying employers, the wrong side of the marketplace for revenue.
Twenty-one analysts average a $20.32 target against a $13.13 price, a 55% gap that reflects how heavily China-listing risk is discounted rather than disagreement about the business.
opportunities: The shares trade at about 9.4 times earnings and 5.7 times EV/EBITDA for a business with a 33% net margin and a dominant market position.
Cash of $1.9B against $22.6M of debt is more than a quarter of the entire market value, held in net cash.
Revenue has grown strongly since the downturn, from $654.0M in 2022 to $1.2B in 2025.
Free cash flow of $677.0M against a $6.2B market value is a very high yield for a company still growing at this rate.
Any recovery in Chinese private-sector hiring flows almost directly into revenue, because the cost base is already built.
watch: Paying enterprise customers, not users. Candidate numbers rise when the job market is bad; paying employers rise when it is good, and that is the side of the marketplace that generates revenue.
view: Strip away the jurisdiction for a moment and look at what this business is. BOSS Zhipin is the dominant online recruitment marketplace in the world’s second-largest economy, with a 33% net margin, $677 million of free cash flow, $1.9 billion of net cash against a $6.2 billion market value, and revenue that has nearly doubled in three years. It trades at 9.4 times earnings and 5.7 times EV/EBITDA. A business with those characteristics listed in the United States would trade at three or four times that multiple, and everyone looking at this stock knows it.

The product advantage is real and worth understanding, because it explains the market share. Traditional recruitment sites take a CV and drop it into a company’s applicant tracking system, where it may sit unread for weeks. BOSS Zhipin puts the candidate into a chat with the actual hiring manager. That single design decision produces dramatically faster responses, which is what both sides of the market actually want, and it created the network effect that now protects the company: employers advertise where the candidates are, candidates go where the employers are, and nobody has broken that loop.

So why is it cheap? Two reasons, and only one of them is about the business. The first is cyclical: Chinese private-sector hiring has been weak, youth unemployment is high, and that is precisely the wrong combination for a recruitment marketplace — lots of candidates, fewer employers willing to pay. Revenue went nowhere in 2022 for exactly this reason. That is a genuine headwind and also a self-correcting one, because when hiring recovers the revenue flows straight through a cost base that is already built.

The second reason is the one that actually sets the multiple, and it is not something analysis can resolve. These shares are a US-listed claim on a holding company structure over Chinese operating entities, in a sector that holds enormous quantities of personal data, in a regulatory environment that has previously demonstrated it can reprice an entire industry in a week. The twenty-one analysts averaging $20.32, some 55% above the market, are not disagreeing with me about the business; they are applying a smaller discount for that risk than the market is. My view is that the operating business is excellent and clearly undervalued on its fundamentals, and that the discount exists for a reason you cannot diligence away. That makes it a legitimate position sized for the possibility that the discount never closes, rather than a mispricing waiting to be corrected.
bull: Chinese private-sector hiring recovers into a cost base already built, revenue and margins expand together, and the structural discount narrows even partially.
bear: Hiring stays weak while regulatory or listing risk reasserts itself, and a cheap multiple on a good business stays cheap indefinitely or worse.
